title: Bryan Johnson's Blueprint Protocol, as Published
description: Bryan Johnson's Blueprint routine as listed on his own protocol page (checked 29 Sept 2026), with the evidence status of each element. Bloomberg reported a cost of about $2 million a year in 2023, per Wikipedia.
longDescription: Bryan Johnson sold Braintree to PayPal (announced 2013 at $800 million, per Wikipedia) and now publishes a daily routine called Blueprint at protocol.bryanjohnson.com. This page lists what his protocol page states, checked on 29 Sept 2026. The biomarker results are self-reported by a founder who sells related products, and no independent trial has tested the combination. It is description, not advice, and not a suggestion to copy any element.
approach: A published daily routine of fixed timing, exercise, diet, supplements and prescription medicines, with self-reported test results
keyPhilosophy: Last meal at noon, about 2,250 calories a day, described on his page as 10% calorie restriction
Six hours of exercise a week: three strength sessions and three cardio sessions
Results are published on his own page and are not independently verified

sections.title: Morning supplements (as listed on his page)
sections.description: Johnson's protocol page lists a morning stack of his own branded products plus creatine, collagen, olive oil, omega-3 and an adaptogen blend. Doses below are what his page states, not recommendations.

items.name: Longevity Mix
items.dose: Per his protocol page: listed, amount not stated here
items.purpose: A branded multi-ingredient powder sold by Johnson's company
items.evidenceNote: Proprietary mix sold by his own company; we have not verified its contents or any effect.

items.name: Creatine Monohydrate
items.purpose: Listed in his morning stack
items.evidenceNote: Creatine has the strongest human evidence in this stack for exercise performance; see the graded supplement ladder on this site.

items.name: Collagen Peptides
items.timing: Morning; a further scoop at noon
items.purpose: Listed in his morning stack

items.name: Extra Virgin Olive Oil
items.purpose: Listed in his stack
items.evidenceNote: Johnson sells his own olive oil brand; that is a commercial interest.

items.name: EPA/DHA Omega-3
items.purpose: Listed in his morning stack
items.evidenceNote: A large trial of ordinary fish-oil capsules (VITAL) found no reduction in major cardiovascular events; see the supplement ladder.

items.name: Ashwagandha & Rhodiola
items.purpose: Listed in his morning stack

sections.title: Diet: noon cutoff and calories
sections.description: His page describes a last meal at noon and about 2,250 calories a day.

items.name: Noon Food Cutoff
items.dose: Per his protocol page: stops eating around noon
items.purpose: Time-restricted eating
items.evidenceNote: In a 139-person randomised trial in people with obesity (NEJM 2022), time restriction did not beat ordinary calorie restriction for weight loss or metabolic markers.

items.name: Calorie Restriction, about 10%
items.dose: Per his protocol page: 2,250 kcal/day, described as 10% restriction; 130 g protein, 206 g carbohydrate, 101 g fat
items.purpose: Mild calorie restriction
items.evidenceNote: The CALERIE trial used 25% restriction for two years and found a slower DunedinPACE measure but no significant change in PhenoAge or GrimAge; his level is lower than the trial's.

sections.title: Exercise (as listed on his page)
sections.description: His page lists six hours of exercise a week.

items.name: Strength and cardio
items.dose: Per his protocol page: 6 hours a week: 3 strength and 3 cardio sessions
items.purpose: Strength and cardiorespiratory fitness
items.evidenceNote: A cohort of 122,007 patients found the lowest fitness group had about five times the mortality of the elite group (JAMA Netw Open 2018); it is observational.

items.name: Zone 2 and vigorous cardio
items.dose: Per his protocol page: 150 min moderate (zone 2) and 75 min vigorous per week
items.purpose: Aerobic base and high-intensity work

sections.title: Recovery therapies (as listed on his page)
sections.description: His page lists sauna, hyperbaric oxygen, red light and shockwave sessions. Outcomes quoted are self-reported single-person results, not a controlled trial.

items.name: Dry Sauna
items.dose: Per his protocol page: 175 F (about 79 C), 20 minutes, daily, with ice protection
items.purpose: Heat exposure

items.name: Red and Near-Infrared Light Therapy
items.dose: Per his protocol page: 6 minutes, twice a day
items.purpose: Photobiomodulation
items.evidenceNote: See the red light evidence page: support for some hair and skin outcomes, none for strength in healthy people.

items.name: Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT)
items.dose: Per his protocol page: 60 sessions, 5 a week, 90 minutes each, 100% oxygen at 2 atmospheres
items.purpose: Oxygen at raised pressure
items.evidenceNote: His page reports after 60 sessions a 2.6% telomere length increase, telomerase activity at an age-12 equivalent, hsCRP below detectable levels, a 28.6% pTAU217 reduction and a 300% VEGF increase. These are self-reported results from one person with no control group; read as hypothesis-generating, not proof.

items.name: Shockwave Therapy
items.dose: Per his protocol page: 4,500 shocks, level 14, 3 times a week
items.purpose: Listed on his page

sections.title: Sleep and skin (as listed on his page)
sections.description: His page lists a fixed sleep schedule and a skin routine.

items.name: Sleep Timing
items.dose: Per his protocol page: 8:30 pm bedtime, about 5:00 am wake
items.purpose: Fixed sleep schedule

items.name: Skin routine with tretinoin
items.dose: Per his protocol page: tretinoin 0.025 to 0.1%
items.purpose: Skin routine
items.evidenceNote: Prescription strength products need a prescriber. His page reports a skin age of 40 at age 44 and 39 at age 48, self-reported.

sections.title: Self-reported results
sections.description: These figures are published by Johnson on his own protocol page and have not been independently verified. We could not find a DunedinPACE value on the page on 29 Sept 2026, so any specific figure quoted elsewhere should be treated as unverified.

items.name: Biomarker and fitness percentiles
items.dose: Per his protocol page: muscle 98th percentile; bone density 99th percentile; grip strength top 5%
items.purpose: Self-reported by a founder who sells related products
items.evidenceNote: One person, no control group; not evidence the routine causes these results.

items.name: Reported cost
items.dose: Bloomberg reported about $2 million a year (2023)
items.purpose: Third-party report, not confirmed on his page
items.evidenceNote: His page says only that he has spent millions of dollars; the exact total is not stated there.

estimatedCost: Not published by Johnson; Bloomberg reported about $2 million a year in 2023 (via Wikipedia)
disclaimer: This page describes one person's published protocol, checked on 29 Sept 2026, and is not advice. Several elements are prescription medicines taken under his own physicians; do not copy any prescription or medical procedure without a doctor. Johnson is an experiment of one, not a clinical trial, and his results are self-reported.

faq.question: How much does Bryan Johnson spend on his Blueprint protocol?
faq.answer: Bloomberg reported a cost of around $2 million a year in 2023 (as relayed by Wikipedia). His own protocol page says only that he has spent millions of dollars and gives no exact figure.

faq.question: What is Bryan Johnson's biological age?
faq.answer: His protocol page reports a skin age of 39 at chronological age 48 and several fitness percentiles. These are self-reported and not independently verified. We could not find a DunedinPACE value on his page on 29 Sept 2026.

faq.question: What supplements does Bryan Johnson take?
faq.answer: His page lists a morning stack of branded products (Longevity Mix, Essentials capsules, antioxidants, protein) plus creatine, collagen peptides, olive oil, EPA/DHA and an ashwagandha and rhodiola capsule. Wikipedia reports that he cut his daily supplements from 111 to 30 by March 2026. This describes his routine and is not a recommendation.

title: Huberman's Supplement Protocol (2025)
description: Stanford neuroscientist Andrew Huberman's complete supplement stack — from his AG1 morning foundation and sleep stack to his testosterone support protocol and cognitive performance compounds.
longDescription: Dr. Andrew Huberman is a Professor of Neurobiology and Ophthalmology at Stanford School of Medicine. His Huberman Lab podcast reaches 50+ million monthly listeners and has done more to popularise evidence-based health tools than perhaps any media platform in history. His philosophy is behaviour-first: morning sunlight, cold exposure, NSDR, and sleep quality precede any supplement recommendation. Huberman has updated his stack significantly in 2024–2025 — adding grape seed extract and boron, cycling out consistent NMN use, and refining his testosterone support protocol.
role: Professor of Neurobiology, Stanford School of Medicine. Host of Huberman Lab podcast.
approach: Behaviour-first neuroscience — foundational behaviours (light, sleep, exercise, stress) before supplements
keyPhilosophy: Foundational behaviours first: morning sunlight, quality sleep, Zone 2 exercise, breathwork
Delay caffeine 90–120 minutes after waking to allow adenosine clearance — avoids afternoon energy crash
Non-sleep deep rest (NSDR / Yoga Nidra) for 10–20 min daily — as effective as sleep for dopamine restoration
Supplements are "tools for the specific job" — not a foundation, not magic
Cold exposure 3–5x/week as a deliberate stress inoculation practice
Testosterone is modifiable: sleep, training, stress management, and targeted supplementation all move the needle

sections.title: Daily Foundation
sections.description: Huberman's consistent daily stack — taken year-round regardless of circumstances.

items.name: AG1 (Athletic Greens)
items.purpose: Comprehensive micronutrient foundation — greens, probiotics, adaptogens, enzymes. Huberman has been a paid partner since 2021.
items.evidenceNote: AG1 is a disclosed sponsorship. Independently: useful as a micronutrient insurance policy, particularly for those with inconsistent vegetable intake. Not a substitute for whole food nutrition.

items.name: Omega-3 (EPA/DHA)
items.purpose: Mood, cognition, cardiovascular health, anti-inflammation. Huberman calls this the supplement he would take if he could only take one.

items.name: Vitamin D3
items.purpose: Immune function, mood, testosterone support, bone health. Huberman tests his levels and adjusts dose to maintain 50–70 ng/mL.

items.name: Creatine Monohydrate
items.purpose: Muscle performance, cognitive function, brain protection. Huberman added creatine to his daily stack in 2023 after reviewing the cognitive evidence.

items.name: Grape Seed Extract
items.purpose: Vascular function — OPCs in grape seed extract support endothelial health and nitric oxide production
items.evidenceNote: Huberman added this in 2024. Moderately evidenced for blood pressure and vascular function.

items.name: Opti-Men Multivitamin
items.purpose: Micronutrient insurance — covers gaps in B vitamins, minerals, and trace elements
items.evidenceNote: Huberman uses a high-potency multivitamin on days when AG1 is not available, or in combination.

sections.title: Sleep Stack
sections.description: Huberman's most requested protocol — the sleep stack he takes nightly. Emphasis: these supplements improve sleep onset and quality, not quantity. Sleep hygiene comes first.

items.name: Magnesium L-Threonate or Bisglycinate
items.purpose: GABA modulation, sleep onset, cognitive protection. L-Threonate crosses the blood-brain barrier; bisglycinate provides better GI tolerance.

items.name: Apigenin
items.purpose: Mild anxiolytic — binds GABA-A receptors. Found naturally in chamomile. Reduces anxiety without sedation.
items.evidenceNote: Huberman considers this a "subtle but real" sleep-onset aid. Modest clinical evidence but very safe. Not recommended if prone to vivid dreams.

items.name: L-Theanine
items.purpose: Alpha wave induction — calming without sedation. Synergistic with magnesium for sleep onset.
items.evidenceNote: Huberman cautions: do NOT take L-Theanine if prone to vivid or intense dreams — it significantly amplifies dream vividness in some people. Start at 100mg to test.

items.name: Glycine
items.purpose: Core body temperature reduction, sleep quality, collagen synthesis
items.evidenceNote: Occasional addition for Huberman — not every night. Glycine lowers core body temperature which facilitates sleep onset. Safe, low cost.

items.name: GABA (occasional)
items.purpose: GABAergic calming — Huberman uses rarely, primarily during high-stress periods
items.evidenceNote: Huberman is cautious about GABA supplementation becoming habitual. Uses situationally.

sections.title: Testosterone & Hormone Support
sections.description: Huberman's testosterone optimisation protocol — focusing on evidence-based compounds that support the HPG axis without testosterone replacement.

items.name: Tongkat Ali (Longjack)
items.purpose: Stimulates LH (luteinising hormone) release → increases endogenous testosterone production. Reduces SHBG.
items.evidenceNote: Huberman considers this the most evidence-backed natural testosterone support supplement. 3+ human RCTs showing meaningful T increases in deficient men.

items.name: Fadogia Agrestis
items.purpose: LH stimulation through different mechanism than Tongkat Ali — potentially additive effect
items.evidenceNote: Huberman cycles: 8 weeks on, 2 weeks off. Fewer human studies than Tongkat Ali. Huberman advocates cycling to prevent LH receptor desensitisation.

items.name: Zinc
items.purpose: Essential cofactor for testosterone synthesis and immune function. Deficiency directly suppresses testosterone.
items.evidenceNote: Huberman recommends testing zinc status. Only supplement if deficient or borderline. Essential during high training loads when zinc losses increase via sweat.

items.name: Boron
items.purpose: Reduces SHBG, increases free testosterone, supports bone density and joint health
items.evidenceNote: Added to Huberman's protocol in 2024. Small human studies show boron supplementation reduces SHBG by 20–25%, meaningfully increasing free testosterone.

sections.title: Focus & Cognitive Performance
sections.description: Situational supplements for demanding cognitive work — not taken daily.

items.name: Alpha-GPC
items.purpose: Acetylcholine precursor — enhances focus, working memory, and learning consolidation
items.evidenceNote: Huberman cycles this — not daily. Excessive acetylcholine can cause brain fog in some. 300mg is conservative. Used on high-output creative or analytical work days.

items.name: L-Tyrosine
items.timing: 30 min before demanding or stressful tasks
items.purpose: Dopamine and norepinephrine precursor — motivation, focus under pressure, stress resilience
items.evidenceNote: Context-dependent. Huberman notes L-Tyrosine is most effective for maintaining performance under stress — not for baseline performance in low-stress conditions.

items.name: Caffeine
items.purpose: Adenosine antagonist — enhanced alertness, physical performance
items.evidenceNote: Critical timing note: Huberman delays caffeine 90 min to allow natural adenosine clearance. Immediate caffeine just delays the adenosine crash — delaying it eliminates the crash entirely. This is one of his most popularised "tools".

items.name: Ashwagandha KSM-66
items.purpose: Cortisol reduction, HPG axis support, sleep quality
items.evidenceNote: Huberman cycles ashwagandha — uses during stressful periods, takes breaks. Cycles prevent HPA axis adaptation.

disclaimer: Huberman's protocol evolves frequently — always check his current podcast episodes for updates. AG1 is a paid sponsorship. Fadogia Agrestis has limited human safety data — Huberman himself recommends cycling and monitoring.

title: David Sinclair's Longevity Protocol (2025)
description: Harvard genetics professor David Sinclair's evolving supplement stack — updated with his June 2025 interview data. NMN, resveratrol, fisetin (kept), quercetin (dropped), berberine replacing metformin, and new additions.
longDescription: Dr. David Sinclair is Professor of Genetics at Harvard Medical School and co-director of the Paul F. Glenn Center for Biology of Aging Research. His 2019 book Lifespan and his Information Theory of Aging established him as the most widely read longevity scientist in the world. His protocol has evolved significantly from the one described in Lifespan: he dropped quercetin in 2023 (new research suggested SIRT6/NRF2 interference), largely replaced metformin with berberine (GI tolerance), added rapamycin quarterly, and added nattokinase and spermidine to his stack.
role: Professor of Genetics, Harvard Medical School. Author of Lifespan.
approach: Information Theory of Aging — restore epigenetic information that drives youthful gene expression via sirtuins, NAD+, and senolytics
keyPhilosophy: Aging is a disease — and like all diseases, it can be treated and reversed
The Information Theory of Aging: cells lose epigenetic information over time; restoring it is the key to reversing aging
NAD+ is the master regulator — sirtuins require it; restoring declining NAD+ (via NMN) is central to his longevity strategy
Xenohormesis: compounds made by stressed plants (resveratrol, fisetin, quercetin) activate our own survival pathways
Skips breakfast daily — fasting activates AMPK, sirtuins, and autophagy that food shuts down
Dropped quercetin (2023), dropped metformin (largely), added rapamycin quarterly — the protocol evolves with evidence

sections.title: Core Morning Stack
sections.description: Sinclair's primary daily supplements — unchanged for years at their core, though doses and additions have evolved.

items.name: NMN
items.purpose: NAD+ restoration — Sinclair was instrumental in popularising NMN as the primary NAD+ precursor
items.evidenceNote: Sinclair takes 1g — twice to four times higher than typical clinical trial doses (250–500mg). He argues higher doses are warranted given the steep NAD+ decline with age.

items.name: Resveratrol
items.timing: Morning with olive oil or yogurt — fat required for absorption
items.purpose: SIRT1 activator — core of Sinclair's sirtuin activation strategy. Synergistic with NMN.
items.evidenceNote: Resveratrol's human evidence is more contested than Sinclair's own enthusiasm suggests. He acknowledges the human RCT data is mixed — but continues based on mechanistic plausibility and his own biomarkers.

items.name: Berberine
items.purpose: AMPK activator — largely replaced metformin. Similar mechanism, better GI tolerance, no prescription required.
items.evidenceNote: Sinclair switched from metformin primarily due to GI side effects. Berberine activates AMPK through a slightly different mechanism (mitochondrial complex I inhibition vs. metformin's direct AMPK activation).

items.name: Vitamin D3 + K2
items.purpose: Immune function, bone health, cancer risk reduction — Sinclair considers vitamin D deficiency a significant longevity risk

items.name: Omega-3
items.purpose: Cardiovascular protection, anti-inflammatory, brain health

items.name: Alpha-Lipoic Acid
items.purpose: Mitochondrial antioxidant, glucose disposal, heavy metal chelation
items.evidenceNote: Part of Sinclair's antioxidant stack. R-ALA form is significantly better absorbed than racemic ALA.

items.name: CoQ10
items.purpose: Mitochondrial electron transport, lipid-soluble antioxidant

sections.title: Senolytics & Autophagy
sections.description: Sinclair's updated senolytic protocol — quercetin dropped in 2023, fisetin retained, spermidine added for autophagy.

items.name: Fisetin
items.purpose: Senolytic — clears senescent cells. Retained after dropping quercetin in 2023. More potent senolytic than quercetin in mouse studies.
items.evidenceNote: Sinclair dropped quercetin in 2023 after research suggested possible SIRT6 and NRF2 pathway interference. Fisetin does not have this concern and shows stronger senolytic activity in animal models.

items.name: Spermidine
items.purpose: Autophagy inducer — triggers cellular self-cleaning. Found in aged cheese, wheat germ, mushrooms.
items.evidenceNote: Sinclair added spermidine after 2022 human studies showed cognitive protection and cardiovascular benefits. The mechanistic case (autophagy induction) is strong; long-term human RCTs are emerging.

items.name: Nattokinase
items.timing: Away from food (best absorbed on empty stomach)
items.purpose: Fibrinolytic enzyme from fermented soybeans — reduces fibrin and clot formation. Emerging cardiovascular data.
items.evidenceNote: Sinclair added nattokinase in 2023. Mechanistically interesting for cardiovascular risk. Human trial data growing but not yet conclusive.

sections.title: Prescription & Quarterly Interventions
sections.description: Sinclair's pharmacological longevity interventions — some quarterly pulsed, some daily.

items.name: Rapamycin
items.purpose: mTOR inhibition — Sinclair uses a quarterly pulsed protocol rather than a weekly continuous approach
items.evidenceNote: Rx only. Sinclair argues that intermittent rapamycin may capture mTOR inhibition benefits while minimising immunosuppression. This is a contentious area — the optimal dosing frequency is genuinely unknown.

items.name: Low-dose Aspirin
items.purpose: Anti-inflammatory, cardiovascular protection — Sinclair continues despite updated cardiology guidance against routine aspirin in healthy adults
items.evidenceNote: Rx-free but contested. Updated AHA/ACC guidelines (2022) no longer recommend aspirin for primary prevention in most adults. Sinclair continues based on his personal risk assessment.

items.name: Statin
items.purpose: Aggressive ApoB/LDL-C lowering for cardiovascular risk reduction
items.evidenceNote: Rx only. Sinclair is explicit about treating cholesterol aggressively. He views cardiovascular disease as the most preventable of the "four horsemen" of aging.

items.name: Metformin (occasional)
items.purpose: AMPK activation — Sinclair reduced metformin use due to GI side effects but has not entirely eliminated it
items.evidenceNote: Rx only. Sinclair has not publicly abandoned metformin — he uses it more sporadically than previously. The berberine switch is largely pragmatic (GI tolerance) rather than philosophical.

sections.title: Lifestyle & Fasting
sections.description: Sinclair's non-supplement longevity practices — which he argues are equal in importance to his pill protocol.

items.name: Intermittent Fasting (skip breakfast)
items.dose: First meal at 1–2 PM, last meal 8–9 PM
items.purpose: AMPK activation, sirtuin activation, autophagy induction, IGF-1 reduction. Sinclair has skipped breakfast for a decade.
items.evidenceNote: Sinclair's IGF-1 is reported at 40% below population average — consistent with reduced mTOR/IGF-1 signalling that animal longevity models associate with extended lifespan.

items.name: Cold Exposure
items.dose: 2–3x/week cold shower or brief outdoor cold
items.purpose: Xenohormesis — mild stress activates survival pathways. Norepinephrine release, mitochondrial biogenesis.
items.evidenceNote: Sinclair frames cold exposure as a form of xenohormesis — the same concept as plant polyphenols activating human survival pathways.

items.name: Plant-heavy, Low Red Meat Diet
items.purpose: Reduce IGF-1 signalling (mTOR inhibition via lower amino acid load), increase polyphenol intake, gut microbiome diversity
items.evidenceNote: Sinclair's dietary approach conflicts with high-protein strategies favoured by some other longevity physicians. The core tension: anti-sarcopenic protein intake versus mTOR inhibition. Both have valid mechanistic cases.

disclaimer: Sinclair's protocol has changed significantly since Lifespan was published in 2019 — always use current interview data, not the book. Rapamycin, statins, and metformin require prescriptions. The scientific community has ongoing debates about several of Sinclair's claims, particularly resveratrol's human efficacy.
